nitnem.title: Nitnem, with your place kept
nitnem.body: The daily banis by time of day — Japji, Jaap, Savaiye, Chaupai and Anand in the morning, Rehras at dusk, Sohila at night — with Sukhmani, Asa di Vaar and Ardaas alongside. The app remembers where you are in each and keeps a quiet record of the days you read. Reminders are optional, local, and yours to set.

watch.body: The day is divided into eight pahars, and different raags belong to different watches. The Raag Clock shows which belong to this one — by fixed hours, or by your local sunrise and sunset. The deep night is left in silence.

widgets.title: On your Home Screen and Lock Screen
widgets.body: Three widgets: the raag of the moment, the Hukam of the day with its Ang, and today's Nitnem — in sizes from small to large, with Lock Screen accessories for the raag and the Nitnem. The Hukam of the day is one complete Hukam for the whole day, chosen by the date: the same in the app and in Siri, with its opening verse on the widget. An optional Live Activity shows how far you have read a bani. It never shows a verse.
widgets.detail: Ask Siri for “Today’s Hukam”, “What raag is it now”, “Read a Vaar”, “Open a theme” or “Open a voice”. Spotlight finds your saved verses and every theme.

verbatim.body: The text is reproduced character for character from the source edition. Nothing is normalised, modernised or improved.
verbatim.reconciledBody: All {characters} characters are proven against the source edition, character for character — zero loss.
verbatim.sealedBody: The bundled text carries a SHA-256 checksum, fixed when the app is built.
verbatim.checkedBody: The app checks it when it is installed or updated. If a check fails, the app refuses to show the text rather than risk showing it altered.

features.madeForReadingNot: Made for reading, not for scrolling
features.theWholeGranthThe: The whole Granth, the daily banis and the study tools — quiet, exact, and entirely on your device. No feeds, no accounts, nothing asking for your attention.
features.readerOnIpadIn: Reader on iPad in landscape, open at Ang 705 — Gurmukhi in Sant Lipi with transliteration under each line
features.theWholeGranthSet: The whole Granth, set to be read
features.allAngsInSant: All {angs} Angs in Sant Lipi, on warm paper or in a night scheme that is never pure black. Turn pages, jump to any Ang, pick up where you left off. Every composition opens with its printed heading, and transliteration can sit quietly under each line. Sehaj focus leaves only the Gurmukhi, with room to breathe.
features.readerOnIphoneAt: Reader on iPhone at Ang 1400 with traditional saroop off
features.readerOnIphoneAt2: Reader on iPhone at Ang 1400 with traditional saroop on

features.traditionalSaroopDrawsThe: Traditional saroop draws the doubled subjoined ya as the single tucked form used in the printed Bir; turn it off to see the exact source characters. Only the drawing changes — stored text, search and Copy are always the verbatim characters.
features.searchOnIphoneThe: Search on iPhone: the Roman word naam, in Auto mode, finds matching lines with their Ang and voice
features.verifyOnIphoneA: Verify on iPhone: a line typed in Roman letters, confirmed as scripture and shown as its canonical line, Ang 8
features.aWordInGurmukhi: A word in Gurmukhi, a word as it sounds in Roman letters, or just the first letters of each word — the way a line comes back to you. Auto mode works out which you meant.
features.verifyChecksALine: Verify checks a line you were sent against the text and tells you plainly whether it is there, and where.
features.aHukamOpenOn: A Hukam open on iPhone: a complete shabad in Raag Kalyan, Ang 1319, with its Rahao line marked and a button to open the Ang in the Reader
features.theHukamOfThe: The Hukam of the day, or a fresh one
features.theHukamOfThe2: The Hukam of the day is one complete Hukam for the whole day, chosen by the date — the same in the app and when you ask Siri, and the Hukam of the day widget shows its opening verse with its Ang. When you want another, draw a fresh one.
features.eitherWayItIs: Either way it is a complete unit — a whole shabad, or a Vaar's pauri with the saloks set before it — never a fragment, read verbatim and cited by its Ang. One tap takes you to that Ang in the Reader.
features.theHukamOfThe3: The Hukam of the day is chosen on your device by the date. It is not the Hukamnama issued from Sri Harmandir Sahib.
features.nitnemOnIpadIn: Nitnem on iPad in landscape: the morning banis with progress rings, and the full list by time of day
features.nitnemReadingJourneyOn: Nitnem reading journey on iPhone: the calendar where the days you read are kept
features.theDailyBanisBy: The daily banis by time of day — Japji, Jaap, Savaiye, Chaupai and Anand in the morning, Rehras at dusk, Sohila at night — with Sukhmani, Asa di Vaar and Ardaas alongside. The app remembers where you are in each.
features.shortLineBanisSuch: Short-line banis such as Jaap, Chaupai and Savaiye are set two half-lines to a row, as in a gutka. Rehras follows the SGPC Nitnem Gutka or the longer Damdami Taksal reading — your choice. Make your own sets, and a reading journey keeps a quiet record of the days you read. Reminders are optional, local, and yours to set.
features.banisFromSriGuru: Banis from Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji come from the same verified corpus, cited by Ang. Dasam Granth and Ardaas text are a separate, labelled, scholar-reviewed layer.
features.raagClockOnIphone: Raag Clock on iPhone, fixed hours: the 2nd pahar of day, 9 am to 12 pm
features.raagClockOnIphone2: Raag Clock on iPhone, solar mode: the watch computed from local sunrise and sunset
features.theDayIsDivided: The day is divided into eight pahars, and different raags belong to different watches. The Raag Clock shows which belong to this one — by fixed hours, or by your local sunrise and sunset, worked out on the device. The deep night is left in silence.
features.theVaarsCountedAs: The Vaars, counted as the Granth prints them
features.allVaarsEachWith: All {vaars} Vaars, each with its voices: who wrote the pauris, and whose saloks are set beside them. The weave lays a Vaar out in reading order, pauri by pauri and salok by salok, as the Granth prints it.
features.theReaderCarriesYou: The reader carries you through a whole Vaar and keeps your place. Show the pauris only, and the saloks are hidden, never removed.
features.askSiriToRead: Ask Siri to “Read a Vaar”, or reach the Vaars from a raag's page in the Index.
features.anIndexThatFollows: An Index that follows the saroop
features.theIndexLaysThe: The Index lays the Granth out in the order of the saroop: a ribbon from Ang 1 to Ang {angs}, the major compositions with your place kept, and all {raags} raags. Every raag has its own page — where it sits in the Granth, the voices in it, the forms its headings name, and the time tradition gives it.
features.inThisHourGathers: “In this hour” gathers the raags of the current watch. Find in Index goes straight to a raag, a bani, a composition or a voice, and Forms lists the poetic forms the printed headings name.
features.aRaagSTraditional: A raag's traditional time is tradition, not scripture — the app says so, and names the source of every claim.
features.themesTracesIdeasAcross: Themes traces ideas across the whole Granth by the words that carry them, with a theme of the day at the top. Every theme has its own page: the Rahao lines that carry it, where it lives by raag and by voice, the forms of its words, and the themes it often appears with — and a verse list you can narrow to a single word form.
features.yourThemesShowsWhich: Your themes shows which themes your saved verses carry. It is worked out on your device, never sent anywhere, and you can turn it off.
features.aThemeSNumber: A theme's number counts the verses that carry its words — never a measure of importance. Themes are also in Spotlight, and Siri can “Open a theme”.
features.lineageFollowsEveryVoice: Lineage follows every voice whose Bani is in the Granth — the Gurus, the Bhagats, the court Bhatts and the Gursikh companions — from the {voiceCenturies}, as a roll or as a river through time, with a voice of the day. Every voice has a page: their Bani in the Granth and its raags, their notable Banis, how they sign their verses, who they name and who names them, their distinctive words, and the voices they echo. Compare sets two side by side.
features.inInsightsTheGranth: In Insights, the Granth becomes a field of dots, one for about 50 lines, coloured by tradition, and a ribbon shows where each voice sings.
features.whoWroteEachLine: Who wrote each line follows the evidence printed in the Granth: a composition's heading, or the pen-name in its closing verse. Dates are approximate and cited; fuller notes on each life wait for scholarly review and are marked so.

privacy.theAppCollectsNothing: The app collects nothing. Here is exactly what that means.
privacy.appliesToTheGurbani: Applies to the <strong1>Gurbani Soul</strong1> app for iPhone and iPad (bundle <code1>org.sggs.app</code1>, including its widgets and Live Activity) and to this website.
privacy.theAppMakesNo: The app makes <strong1>no network connections</strong1>. It works fully in Airplane Mode.
privacy.noAnalyticsNoAdvertising: No analytics, no advertising, no tracking, no third-party SDKs in the app. This website counts page views anonymously, without cookies; see <link1>This website</link1>.
privacy.savedVersesAreStored: <strong1>Saved verses</strong1> are stored in the app's own database on your device. If you save a verse, it is also added to your device's Spotlight index so you can find it from the Home Screen search; unsaving removes it. Spotlight data stays on your device.
privacy.themesInSpotlightThe: <strong1>Themes in Spotlight</strong1>: the app also adds the {themes} theme names, with their Gurmukhi words and verse counts, to Spotlight so a theme can be opened from the Home Screen search. These entries hold nothing about you.
privacy.yourThemesOnThe: <strong1>Your themes</strong1> on the Themes page is worked out on your device from your saved verses. It is never sent anywhere, and you can turn it off in More (“Show Your themes”).
privacy.settingsAccentColourTransliteration: <strong1>Settings</strong1> (accent colour, transliteration, traditional rendering, last Ang read) are stored in the app's local preferences.
privacy.vaarsWhereYouAre: <strong1>Vaars</strong1>: where you are in a Vaar you are reading is stored in a small file in the app's own App Group container on your device. It is never transmitted.
privacy.nitnemProgressWhereYou: <strong1>Nitnem</strong1> progress (where you are in each bani, which days you completed it, your own sets and journey) is stored in small files in the app's own App Group container on your device, so the Nitnem widget can show it. It is never transmitted.
privacy.remindersAreOptionalLocal: <strong1>Reminders</strong1> are optional local notifications. The app asks for notification permission only when you turn a reminder on, schedules them on your device at the times you choose, and uses no push service: no notification ever comes from a server, and no device token is created or sent anywhere.
privacy.liveActivityIsOptional: <strong1>Live Activity</strong1> is optional and off by default. When you turn it on, a reading session shows its progress on your Lock Screen and in the Dynamic Island. It is driven entirely on your device (no push updates) and never shows a verse.
privacy.widgetsReadASmall: <strong1>Widgets</strong1> read a small snapshot the app writes into its own App Group container on your device: the raag watch, the Hukam of the day for the next two weeks with their Angs, today's Nitnem progress, and — if you use solar mode — your clock-mode choice and the same ~1 km rounded coordinates. Nothing leaves the device.
privacy.locationIsUsedOnly: <strong1>Location</strong1> is used only by the Raag Clock's optional solar mode to compute local sunrise and sunset. It is requested only when you tap “Use my location” in solar mode. The fix is rounded to two decimal places (about 1 km) before it is stored in the app's own App Group container — shared only with the app's widgets on the same device — and the raw position is never kept. You can enter a location manually instead, or deny the permission; the clock still works.
privacy.integrityChecksReadThe: <strong1>Integrity checks</strong1> read the bundled scripture database's size and modification date to decide whether its checksum needs re-verifying. This is why the app's privacy manifest declares the "file timestamp" and "user defaults" API reasons. Nothing is displayed or transmitted.
privacy.diagnosticsIfTheApp: <strong1>Diagnostics</strong1>: if the app ever crashes or hangs, iOS may hand it a diagnostic report. The app writes that report to its own local folder; it is never uploaded. You can see how many there are, share them via the system share sheet to a destination you choose, or delete them under More → About & credits → Integrity — nothing leaves the device unless you send it. Separately, Apple may share crash reports with us through App Store Connect <em1>only</em1> if you have enabled "Share with App Developers" in your iOS Privacy & Security → Analytics settings. Those reports are governed by Apple's privacy policy and contain no account or identity information.
privacy.becauseTheAppCollects: Because the app collects no data, its App Store privacy label is <strong1>"Data Not Collected"</strong1>.
privacy.theGurbaniSoulPages: The Gurbani Soul pages (the home page, Features, The watch, Learn, Support, Contribute and this policy) count page views with <strong1>Vercel Web Analytics</strong1>, and only when served from gurbanisoul.com. It uses no cookies and does not follow you across other sites. It records the page, the referring site, and your country, browser, operating system and device type as anonymous totals; visitors are counted with a short-lived hash that is discarded after a day. We do not build profiles from it or share it.
privacy.ifYouAskTo: If you ask to be told when the app is on the App Store, the email address you type is sent to <strong1>Buttondown</strong1>, which sends that one email. Nothing else is sent with it, and you can unsubscribe from the email itself.
privacy.locationIsUsedOn: <strong1>Location</strong1> is used on this website only if you switch the Raag Clock to solar mode, to work out local sunrise and sunset. Switching the mode on asks for nothing: your browser asks your permission only when you press “Use my location”, or you can type coordinates in yourself. The position is rounded to two decimal places (about 1 km) and kept in your browser's local storage; it is never sent to us or anyone else, and “Forget location” removes it. Without a location, the clock stays on fixed hours.

q1.q: Does the app need an internet connection?
q1.a: No. The whole Granth is bundled inside the app. It never connects to any server, so it works on a flight, in a basement, or with mobile data switched off.

q2.q: Why is there no English translation in the app?
q2.a: The English translation we would like to include is licensed for personal study only, and distributing it through the App Store requires a written licence we do not yet hold. Rather than ship it without permission, the app is Gurmukhi-only, with transliteration. If a licence is granted, the translation will arrive in an update as a separate, clearly labelled layer, never mixed into the scripture.

q3.q: What does the "traditional saroop" toggle do?
q3.a: It changes only how the text is drawn: the doubled subjoined ya () is shown as the single tucked form used in the printed Bir. The stored text, search, and Copy are always the verbatim characters. Turn it off in More → Display to see the exact source characters.

q4.q: Why does the app ask for my location?
q4.a: Only if you tap “Use my location” on the Raag Clock’s solar mode, which times the watches of the day by local sunrise and sunset. The location is rounded to about 1 km, kept only on your device, and never transmitted. You can deny the permission and enter a location manually, or stay in fixed mode. See the <privacy>Privacy Policy</privacy>.

q5.a: In More, under Nitnem, Reminders you can switch on a reminder for each part of the day and choose its time. iOS asks for notification permission the first time you switch one on. Reminders are scheduled on your device; nothing comes from a server. Once you complete that part of the day's Nitnem, that day's reminder is dropped. If reminders do not appear, check Settings → Notifications → Gurbani Soul.

q6.q: What is the Live Activity while reading?
q6.a: An optional progress indicator on the Lock Screen and in the Dynamic Island while you read a bani, so you can return to your place with one tap. It is off by default (turn it on in More, under Nitnem), shows progress only, never a verse, and ends when you finish or leave the bani.

q7.q: Where do the Nitnem banis come from?
q7.a: Banis from Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji are this project's own verified, verbatim corpus, cited by Ang. Bani ordering and the Sri Dasam Granth / Ardaas text come via the ShabadOS open database and are shown as a separate, labelled layer, never presented as part of Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji.

q8.q: What is the Hukam of the day?
q8.a: One complete Hukam for the whole day, chosen on your device by the date: the same unit in the app and when you ask Siri for "Today's Hukam", and the Hukam of the day widget shows its opening verse with its Ang. It is not the Hukamnama issued from Sri Harmandir Sahib. To read another, draw a fresh Hukam; the Hukam of the day stays as it is until the date changes.

q9.a: Open the app once; the widgets read a small snapshot the app writes, including the Hukam of the day for the next two weeks. If they stay empty, check More → About & credits → Integrity and confirm it says "Widget App Group available", then email us with that screen.

q10.q: What is the Integrity section in About?
q10.a: When you install or update the app, it verifies that the bundled scripture database is bit-for-bit the certified one (a SHA-256 checksum). Every launch after that re-checks that the file has not changed and re-runs the structural checks. If verification ever fails, the app refuses to show scripture rather than risk showing altered text. Reinstalling from the App Store fixes a corrupted download.

q11.q: How do I save, share, or find a verse later?
q11.a: Long-press a verse (or use the actions on a verse card) to Save, Copy, Share or Explore related verses. Saved verses appear under More → Saved verses and in your device's Spotlight search. Share cards always carry the Ang citation.

q12.a: The app offers nine Siri shortcuts: "Today's Hukam", "Draw a Hukam", "What raag is it now", "Read a bani", "Read a Vaar", "Search Gurbani", "Show the constellation", "Open a theme" and "Open a voice", and "Open Ang" as a Shortcuts action. Your saved verses and the {themes} themes appear in Spotlight. Links such as sggs://ang/500, sggs://hukam/today, sggs://vaar/1 or sggs://voice/guru-tegh-bahadur-ji open the app directly.

q13.q: Why does a voice's page say "Context pending scholarly review"?
q13.a: Notes that explain the text rather than show it — about a Vaar, a theme, or the fuller story of a voice's life — wait until a scholar has reviewed them, and until then the app does not show them. A voice's page says so where its note is waiting. The verbatim lines, their Ang citations and the counts are shown as usual, and the Gurmukhi itself is never touched by this review.

q14.a: The app supports VoiceOver (each verse is read as one item, in Punjabi, with its Ang), Dynamic Type up to the largest accessibility sizes, Reduce Motion and Increase Contrast. If something is unreadable or unreachable with assistive technology, that is a bug: please tell us.

q15.a: The app runs on iPad in portrait and landscape. It deliberately runs as a single window.
